subject: Mathematics
title: Zara's Area Mystery
hook: Zara uses determinants to calculate land areas from coordinates, uncovering geometry hidden in numbers.

slides.title: Determinants
slides.storyContext: Zara's father is a land surveyor. He has coordinates of a triangular plot but needs its area. Determinants transform coordinates into area instantly.

slides.title: The Land Survey
slides.storyContext: Zara's father has a triangle plot with vertices at (0, 0), (4, 0), (2, 3) in a Delhi suburb. He's marked these with GPS. He asks Zara: what's the area? Dr. Mehra says: determinants give you the answer without the distance formula.

slides.title: Why Zara Needs Determinants
slides.storyContext: Raj shows Zara his old surveying methods: using distance formulas and slope calculations for each side, then Heron's formula. It takes 10 minutes per plot. He says: "Determinants do it in 30 seconds. One formula, one calculation." Zara is intrigued.

points.label: The old way
points.text: Calculate all side lengths, use Heron's formula, wait for the answer.

points.label: The determinant way
points.text: Plug coordinates directly into a matrix formula, compute once, done.

slides.inSimpleWords: Determinants are a shortcut to find area from coordinates instantly.

slides.title: What is a Determinant?
slides.storyContext: Dr. Mehra explains: A determinant is a special number calculated from a square matrix. It encodes information about the matrix's invertibility and geometric scaling.

points.label: Notation
points.text: For a square matrix A, determinant is det(A) or |A|.

points.label: 2×2 determinant
points.text: For A = [[a b], [c d]], det(A) = ad − bc.

points.label: Geometric meaning (2×2)
points.text: det(A) is the signed area of the parallelogram formed by row vectors (or column vectors) of A.

example.problem: Find determinant of A = [[2 3], [1 4]].
example.solution: det(A) = 2·4 − 3·1 = 8 − 3 = 5. The parallelogram formed by [2, 3] and [1, 4] has area 5.

slides.inSimpleWords: A determinant is a number derived from a square matrix. For 2×2, it's ad − bc.

slides.title: Matrix Notation and Structure
slides.storyContext: Before Zara can compute determinants, she must understand how to write and read matrices.

points.label: Rows and columns
points.text: An m×n matrix has m rows and n columns. A square matrix has m = n.

points.label: Element notation
points.text: a_{ij} denotes the element in row i, column j. For A = [[1 2], [3 4]], a_{21} = 3.

points.label: 2×2 example
points.text: A = [[a b], [c d]] is 2 rows, 2 columns. Square.

slides.inSimpleWords: Matrices are grids of numbers. Rows go across, columns go down. Determinants only work on square matrices.

slides.title: Computing a 2×2 Determinant Step-by-Step
slides.storyContext: Zara practices the formula with Raj's first survey matrix.

points.label: Formula
points.text: For A = [[a b], [c d]], det(A) = ad − bc.

points.label: Steps
points.text: Multiply diagonals (top-left × bottom-right), subtract the other diagonal (top-right × bottom-left).

example.problem: Find det of [[3 2], [1 5]].

slides.inSimpleWords: Main diagonal (down-right) minus anti-diagonal (down-left).

slides.title: 3×3 Determinant (Expansion)
slides.storyContext: For Zara's triangle area, she needs a 3×3 determinant. Dr. Mehra teaches expansion by minors.

points.label: Expansion along row 1
points.text: For A = [[a b c], [d e f], [g h i]], det(A) = a(ei − fh) − b(di − fg) + c(dh − eg).

points.label: Minor
points.text: M_{ij} = determinant of 2×2 matrix after removing row i and column j.

points.label: Cofactor
points.text: C_{ij} = (−1)^{i+j} · M_{ij}. Alternating signs.

slides.inSimpleWords: Expand a 3×3 determinant by picking a row, then combine minors with alternating signs.

slides.title: The Minor and Cofactor Dance
slides.storyContext: Dr. Mehra acts out the expansion: "Pick a row. Cover its position. What's left? That's the minor — a 2×2 determinant. Compute it. Now add or subtract using signs (+ − +, − + −, + − +) based on position."

points.label: First position (1,1)
points.text: Positive sign (+). Remove row 1 and column 1. Calculate 2×2 det of what's left.

points.label: Second position (1,2)
points.text: Negative sign (−). Remove row 1 and column 2. Calculate 2×2 det, multiply by −1.

points.label: Third position (1,3)
points.text: Positive sign (+). Remove row 1 and column 3. Calculate 2×2 det.

slides.inSimpleWords: Alternate + and − as you move across the row. Each cofactor is a 2×2 determinant scaled by the sign.

slides.title: 3×3 Determinant Fully Worked
slides.storyContext: Zara computes the determinant of a practice matrix step-by-step.
slides.inSimpleWords: Expand along any row (or column). Each term: element × cofactor. Sum them.

slides.title: Area of a Triangle from Coordinates
slides.storyContext: Zara's triangle has vertices A(0, 0), B(4, 0), C(2, 3). Determinant gives area directly.

points.label: Formula
points.text: Area = (1/2) · |det of [[x₁ y₁ 1], [x₂ y₂ 1], [x₃ y₃ 1]]|.

points.label: Why it works
points.text: The determinant of this augmented matrix (with 1s) scales the area of the triangle by 2. Absolute value ensures positive area.

example.problem: Find area of triangle with vertices (0,0), (4,0), (2,3).

slides.inSimpleWords: Plug triangle vertices into a 3×3 determinant formula, divide by 2, take absolute value — instant area.

image.alt: Area of a Triangle from Coordinates — Determinants

slides.title: Zara's First Survey Success
slides.storyContext: Zara applies the formula to her father's plot: (0,0), (4,0), (2,3). She computes: det = 4·3 − 2·0 = 12. Area = 6 square units. Raj verifies with his old methods — match! Zara saves 9 minutes.

points.label: Setup
points.text: Write coordinates as rows with a 1 in the third column.

points.label: Compute
points.text: Expand the 3×3 determinant.

points.label: Final
points.text: Divide by 2, take absolute value.

slides.inSimpleWords: The determinant method is a fast, reliable way to find triangle area from coordinates.

slides.title: Triangle Area with Negative Coordinates
slides.storyContext: Zara's next plot has vertices at (−1, −1), (2, 1), (0, 3). She applies the formula.

example.problem: Find area of triangle with vertices (−1, −1), (2, 1), (0, 3).

slides.inSimpleWords: Works the same for negative coordinates. Determinant formula handles any real numbers.

slides.title: Properties of Determinants
slides.storyContext: Dr. Mehra shares rules that make calculations faster. Zara uses these shortcuts.

points.label: If two rows are identical
points.text: det(A) = 0. No unique area — degenerate shape.

points.label: If two rows are swapped
points.text: det changes sign. Order matters geometrically.

points.label: If a row is multiplied by k
points.text: det is multiplied by k. Scaling one side scales area by k.

points.label: Multiplicative property
points.text: det(A·B) = det(A)·det(B).

points.label: det(A^T) = det(A)
points.text: Transpose doesn't change determinant.

slides.inSimpleWords: These properties help simplify calculation. Identical rows mean zero area (degenerate). Swapping rows flips the sign.

slides.title: When Two Points Coincide
slides.storyContext: Zara's father marks coordinates (1, 2), (3, 5), (3, 5) — he marks the same point twice by mistake. Zara computes the determinant and gets 0. She realizes: zero area means degenerate. She tells Raj, who fixes the data.

points.label: Two identical rows
points.text: Determinant = 0 always.

points.label: Collinear points
points.text: Three points on the same line also give det = 0.

points.label: Check for errors
points.text: If det = 0 unexpectedly, verify the three points are truly distinct and not collinear.

slides.inSimpleWords: Zero determinant signals degenerate or collinear points — area is zero.

slides.title: Swapping Rows Changes the Sign
slides.storyContext: Zara swaps the order of two vertices in her matrix. She notices the determinant flips from +12 to −12. She computes area as (1/2)|−12| = 6, same as before.

example.problem: Compute det with rows in order: (0,0), (4,0), (2,3) and then reversed: (0,0), (2,3), (4,0). Notice the sign change.
example.solution: First order: det([[0 0 1], [4 0 1], [2 3 1]]) = 12. Swapped: det([[0 0 1], [2 3 1], [4 0 1]]) = −12. The absolute value for area is the same: 6.

slides.inSimpleWords: Swapping rows negates the determinant. But absolute value ensures area is always positive.

slides.title: Cramer's Rule
slides.storyContext: Zara learns a powerful method to solve systems of linear equations using determinants — no inverse needed.

points.label: For 2 equations
points.text: a₁x + b₁y = c₁ and a₂x + b₂y = c₂. x = det([[c₁ b₁], [c₂ b₂]]) / det([[a₁ b₁], [a₂ b₂]]), y = det([[a₁ c₁], [a₂ c₂]]) / det([[a₁ b₁], [a₂ b₂]]).

points.label: General form
points.text: For system A·X = B, x_i = det(A_i) / det(A), where A_i is A with column i replaced by B.

points.label: Condition
points.text: Works only if det(A) ≠ 0 (unique solution exists).

example.problem: Solve 2x + 3y = 8 and x − y = 1 using Cramer's rule.

slides.inSimpleWords: Cramer's rule: replace columns one by one with the constants, calculate determinants, divide. Faster than matrix inverse for small systems.

slides.title: Solving for Coordinates Using Cramer's Rule
slides.storyContext: Zara's father has two line equations from boundary surveys: 3x − 2y = 7 and x + y = 5. Where do they intersect? Cramer's rule finds it instantly.

example.problem: Find intersection of 3x − 2y = 7 and x + y = 5.

slides.inSimpleWords: Replace columns with the right-hand side constants, compute determinants, divide by the main determinant.

slides.title: Collinearity Check
slides.storyContext: Zara's father marks three points on a map. Are they collinear (on a single line)? Determinant tells instantly.

points.label: Idea
points.text: Three points are collinear if and only if the area of the triangle they form is zero.

points.label: Method
points.text: Calculate det of [[x₁ y₁ 1], [x₂ y₂ 1], [x₃ y₃ 1]]. If det = 0, collinear.

example.problem: Are (1,2), (2,4), (3,6) collinear?

slides.inSimpleWords: If three points' determinant is zero, they're on the same line.

slides.title: Real-World Application: Multi-Plot Verification
slides.storyContext: Zara's father needs to verify that three boundary posts are collinear (should be on the same boundary line). He gives Zara their coordinates: (0,1), (2,5), (4,9). She computes the determinant.

example.problem: Verify collinearity: (0,1), (2,5), (4,9).

slides.inSimpleWords: If determinant is 0, points are collinear and the boundary is straight.

slides.title: Challenge: Multi-plot Calculation
slides.storyContext: Zara's father surveyed 2 adjacent triangular plots. Plot 1: (0,0), (5,0), (2,4). Plot 2: (5,0), (8,0), (6.5,4). Find both areas and total.

example.problem: Calculate areas using determinants and find total.

slides.inSimpleWords: Apply the determinant area formula to each triangle separately, then sum.

slides.title: Invertibility and Determinants
slides.storyContext: Dr. Mehra teaches: A square matrix is invertible (has an inverse) if and only if its determinant is non-zero.

points.label: Determinant ≠ 0
points.text: Matrix is invertible. System Ax=b has unique solution.

points.label: Determinant = 0
points.text: Matrix is singular (not invertible). System either has no solution or infinitely many solutions.

points.label: Why it matters
points.text: Cramer's rule requires det(A) ≠ 0. If det(A) = 0, Cramer's rule fails.

slides.inSimpleWords: Non-zero determinant: unique solution exists. Zero determinant: no unique solution.

slides.title: When Cramer's Rule Fails
slides.storyContext: Zara encounters a system where Cramer's rule cannot apply. The equations represent parallel lines (no intersection).

example.problem: Solve: 2x + 4y = 8 and x + 2y = 5 using Cramer's rule.
example.solution: A = [[2 4], [1 2]], det(A) = 2·2 − 4·1 = 4 − 4 = 0. Since det(A) = 0, Cramer's rule doesn't apply. The system is inconsistent (parallel lines, no intersection).

slides.inSimpleWords: If determinant is zero, don't use Cramer's rule. Check if equations are dependent or contradictory.

slides.title: Challenge: System Solving and Verification
slides.storyContext: Zara solves for the intersection of two survey lines using Cramer's rule, then verifies collinearity of three boundary points.

example.problem: Solve 4x + y = 11 and 2x − y = 1. Then verify if (2,3), (3,4), (4,5) are collinear.

slides.inSimpleWords: Combine Cramer's rule for solving systems with collinearity checks using the same determinant machinery.

slides.title: Determinants Beyond 3×3
slides.storyContext: Dr. Mehra mentions: Determinants work for 4×4, 5×5, any n×n matrix. The same principles (expansion by minors, cofactor) apply, though calculations grow complex. Zara's surveywork uses only 2×2 and 3×3, but she understands the concept scales.

points.label: 4×4 determinant
points.text: Expand along a row/column, creating four 3×3 minors. Sum with alternating signs.

points.label: General n×n
points.text: Expand along any row/column. Each minor is (n−1)×(n−1). Recursive until 2×2.

slides.inSimpleWords: Determinant formula works for any square matrix, but computation becomes tedious for large matrices.

slides.title: Applications Summary: All Determinant Uses
slides.storyContext: Zara reflects on all the ways she used determinants: area, collinearity, line intersection, error detection.

example.problem: Summarize: triangle area, collinearity check, line intersection (Cramer), singular matrix detection.
example.solution: Area: (1/2)|det 3×3|. Collinearity: det = 0. Intersection: x = det_x/det, y = det_y/det. Singular: det(A) = 0 → no unique solution. Determinant encodes invertibility and geometric scaling.

slides.inSimpleWords: One formula, many applications: geometry, algebra, and system solving.

slides.title: What Zara Learned
slides.storyContext: Determinants turned Zara into a math surveyor, solving land problems with elegance.

points.text: Determinant: a number from a square matrix. For 2×2: ad−bc.
3×3 determinant: expand by minors along a row, with alternating signs.
Geometric meaning: determinant = signed area (or volume in 3D) of parallelogram (or parallelepiped) formed by matrix rows/columns.
Triangle area = (1/2)|det([[x₁ y₁ 1], [x₂ y₂ 1], [x₃ y₃ 1]])|.
Cramer's rule: solve systems by replacing columns with constants, computing determinants, dividing.
Collinearity: three points are collinear if and only if the determinant of their augmented matrix is zero.

slides.inSimpleWords: Determinants unlock geometry from coordinates. Instant areas, collinearity checks, system solutions.

subject: Mathematics
title: Priya's River Run
hook: Priya's morning run along a river teaches her about smooth curves, sudden breaks, and rates of change.

slides.title: Continuity and Differentiability
slides.storyContext: Priya runs along the Yamuna River. Some stretches are smooth; some have sudden drops (a wall). She realizes: smooth paths have good derivatives, broken paths do not.

slides.title: The River Path
slides.storyContext: Priya's running path elevation: flat for 1 km, then slopes up 45° for 2 km, then flat again. But there's a barrier wall (sudden 2-meter drop) that interrupts the path. The smooth slopes have good tangent lines; the wall breaks continuity.

slides.title: What Makes a Path Smooth?
slides.storyContext: Dev asks Priya: "Your path before the wall was smooth. After the wall, you jumped 2 meters. What's the difference mathematically?" Priya realizes: continuity means no jumps. Differentiability means no corners or kinks.

points.label: Smooth = continuous
points.text: No sudden breaks or jumps in elevation.

points.label: Super-smooth = differentiable
points.text: No corners or kinks. You can draw a unique tangent line at every point.

slides.inSimpleWords: Continuity means connected. Differentiability means smooth with a well-defined slope everywhere.

slides.title: What is Continuity?
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Singh defines: A function f is continuous at x=c if the curve doesn't jump or break at that point.

points.label: Three conditions (all required)
points.text: 1) f(c) is defined. 2) lim_{x→c} f(x) exists. 3) lim_{x→c} f(x) = f(c).

points.label: Geometric intuition
points.text: You can draw the curve without lifting your pen.

points.label: Discontinuity types
points.text: Removable (hole at a point), jump (sudden jump), infinite (asymptote).

example.problem: Is f(x) = {x² if x≠1; 2 if x=1} continuous at x=1?
example.solution: f(1) = 2. lim_{x→1} x² = 1. Since limit ≠ f(1), discontinuous (removable discontinuity — the hole at (1,1) is not filled correctly).

slides.inSimpleWords: Continuous = no jumps, holes, or breaks. The limit from both sides equals the function value at that point.

slides.title: Three Continuity Checks at a Point
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Singh walks through checking all three conditions for a function at a specific point.

example.problem: Is f(x) = x + 1 continuous at x=3?
example.solution: 1) f(3) = 3 + 1 = 4 (defined). 2) lim_{x→3} (x+1) = 4 (exists). 3) The limit equals f(3). Yes, continuous.

slides.inSimpleWords: Check: function value at point, limit approaching the point, do they match?

slides.title: Introduction to Derivatives
slides.storyContext: Dev asks Priya: how fast were you running at the 2 km mark? The answer is the derivative — instantaneous rate of change.

points.label: Definition
points.text: Derivative of f at x=c: f'(c) = lim_{h→0} (f(c+h)−f(c)) / h.

points.label: Geometric meaning
points.text: Slope of the tangent line to the curve at (c, f(c)).

points.label: Notation
points.text: f'(x), df/dx, Df(x) all mean the same thing.

example.problem: Find derivative of f(x) = x² at x=3.

slides.inSimpleWords: Derivative = rate of change, or slope of tangent line. Measures how fast the function is increasing/decreasing at that point.

slides.title: From Average to Instantaneous Rate
slides.storyContext: Priya ran 10 km in 1 hour (average speed 10 km/h). But at the 45-minute mark, was she going 10 km/h? Dev explains: derivative gives the instantaneous speed, shrinking the time interval to zero.

points.label: Average rate
points.text: Total distance / total time. Over an interval.

points.label: Instantaneous rate
points.text: Limit of average rate as interval shrinks. At a single point.

slides.inSimpleWords: As the time interval gets smaller and smaller, the average speed approaches the instantaneous speed.

slides.title: Computing a Derivative from Scratch
slides.storyContext: Priya practices computing f'(x) for a simple function using the limit definition.

example.problem: Find f'(2) for f(x) = 3x + 1 using the limit definition.

slides.inSimpleWords: Plug in (x+h), subtract the original, divide by h, then take the limit as h approaches zero.

slides.title: Rules for Derivatives (Power, Product, Chain)
slides.storyContext: Computing derivatives by definition is slow. Mrs. Singh teaches shortcut rules.

points.label: Power rule
points.text: d/dx [x^n] = n·x^{n-1}.

points.label: Product rule
points.text: d/dx [u·v] = u'·v + u·v'.

points.label: Quotient rule
points.text: d/dx [u/v] = (u'·v − u·v') / v².

example.problem: Find derivative of f(x) = (3x² + 1)·sin(x).
example.solution: Using product rule: f'(x) = (6x)·sin(x) + (3x²+1)·cos(x).

slides.inSimpleWords: Power rule: power goes down, multiply. Product rule: first times derivative of second, plus second times derivative of first. Chain rule: derivative of outer times derivative of inner.

slides.title: Why Derivative Rules Save Time
slides.storyContext: Dev shows Priya: using limits to differentiate f(x) = x⁵ would take 10 lines and algebra. Using the power rule: d/dx[x⁵] = 5x⁴. One second. She's convinced.

points.label: Limit definition
points.text: Exact but slow. Works for understanding.

points.label: Rules (power, product, chain, quotient)
points.text: Fast and practical. Use these for computation.

slides.inSimpleWords: Rules let us differentiate polynomials, products, and composed functions instantly without limits.

slides.title: Power Rule in Action
slides.storyContext: Priya practices the power rule on polynomial terms.

example.problem: Find derivatives: d/dx[x³], d/dx[x^(-2)], d/dx[√x].

slides.inSimpleWords: Bring the power down as a coefficient, subtract 1 from the power.

slides.title: Differentiability and Continuity
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Singh clarifies the relationship: If a function is differentiable (has a derivative), it must be continuous. But continuity doesn't guarantee differentiability.

points.label: Statement
points.text: If f is differentiable at x=c, then f is continuous at x=c.

points.label: Contrapositive
points.text: If f is discontinuous at x=c, then f is not differentiable at x=c.

points.label: Converse is false
points.text: f can be continuous but not differentiable. Example: f(x) = |x| at x=0 (sharp corner, no unique tangent).

example.problem: Is f(x) = |x| differentiable at x=0?
example.solution: f is continuous at 0: lim_{x→0} |x| = 0 = f(0). But: left derivative = lim_{h→0⁻} (−h) / h = −1. Right derivative = lim_{h→0⁺} h / h = 1. Left ≠ Right, so not differentiable.

slides.inSimpleWords: Smooth curve (differentiable) ⟹ connected curve (continuous). But connected doesn't mean smooth — corners exist.

slides.title: Left and Right Derivatives
slides.storyContext: Priya's path has a sharp turn at the barrier wall. Dev explains left and right derivatives.

points.label: Left derivative
points.text: f'₋(c) = lim_{h→0⁻} (f(c+h)−f(c)) / h. Slope from the left.

points.label: Right derivative
points.text: f'₊(c) = lim_{h→0⁺} (f(c+h)−f(c)) / h. Slope from the right.

points.label: Differentiable iff
points.text: f'₋(c) = f'₊(c) and both exist.

example.problem: For f(x) = |x−2|, find left and right derivatives at x=2.
example.solution: f'₋(2) = −1 (slope from left is −1). f'₊(2) = 1 (slope from right is 1). Not differentiable at x=2 (sharp corner).

slides.inSimpleWords: Smooth functions have equal left and right slopes. Sharp corners have different slopes from each side.

slides.title: Derivatives of Common Functions
slides.storyContext: Dev creates a cheat sheet of derivatives Priya will use most often.

points.label: Polynomial
points.text: d/dx[x^n] = n·x^{n-1}. d/dx[c] = 0.

points.label: Trigonometric
points.text: d/dx[sin(x)] = cos(x). d/dx[cos(x)] = −sin(x). d/dx[tan(x)] = sec²(x).

points.label: Exponential and logarithm
points.text: d/dx[e^x] = e^x. d/dx[ln(x)] = 1/x. d/dx[a^x] = a^x·ln(a).

slides.inSimpleWords: Memorize these basic derivatives. Use them with power, product, and chain rules for complex functions.

slides.title: Derivatives of Trigonometric Functions
slides.storyContext: Priya's cyclic running motion is described by sine and cosine. She learns their derivatives.

example.problem: Position: s(t) = 10·sin(t). Find velocity and acceleration.
example.solution: v(t) = s'(t) = 10·cos(t). a(t) = v'(t) = −10·sin(t). The acceleration is proportional to negative position — simple harmonic motion.

slides.inSimpleWords: Sine differentiates to cosine. Cosine differentiates to negative sine. They cycle forever.

slides.title: Higher-Order Derivatives
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Singh introduces: the derivative of a derivative is called the second derivative, and so on.

example.problem: For f(x) = x⁴ − 2x³ + x, find f'(x), f''(x), and f'''(x).
example.solution: f'(x) = 4x³ − 6x² + 1. f''(x) = 12x² − 12x. f'''(x) = 24x − 12. These describe rate of change, curvature, and how curvature changes.

slides.inSimpleWords: First derivative: slope. Second derivative: curvature. Third derivative: change in curvature.

slides.title: Priya Spots the Sharp Turn
slides.storyContext: Priya runs up to the wall at (2, 0) then jumps down. The path function f(x) = |x−2| has a sharp corner at x=2. From the left, she's going downhill at −45°. From the right, she's going uphill at +45°. Left derivative ≠ right derivative.

points.label: Before the wall
points.text: Slope = −1 (moving down-left to the wall).

points.label: After the wall
points.text: Slope = +1 (moving up-right from the wall).

points.label: At the wall
points.text: No unique tangent line — corner exists.

slides.inSimpleWords: Corners and kinks break differentiability because the slope changes abruptly.

slides.title: Instantaneous Velocity Problem
slides.storyContext: Priya's position at time t (in hours) is s(t) = t² (distance in km). What is her instantaneous velocity at t=2?

points.label: Position function
points.text: s(t) = t².

example.problem: Find instantaneous velocity at t=2 hours.
example.solution: v(2) = 2(2) = 4 km/hour. At the 2-hour mark, Priya is running at 4 km/hour.

slides.inSimpleWords: Derivative of position gives velocity. Tells you speed at a specific instant.

slides.title: Piecewise Function: Checking Continuity
slides.storyContext: Priya's elevation map is piecewise: flat at 10 m for the first 2 km, then rising linearly. Check continuity at the junction (x=2).

example.problem: f(x) = {10 if x < 2; 5 + 2x if x ≥ 2}. Continuous at x=2?
example.solution: f(2) = 5 + 2(2) = 9. lim_{x→2⁻} 10 = 10. lim_{x→2⁺} (5+2x) = 9. Left limit ≠ right limit ≠ f(2), so discontinuous (jump of 1 meter).

slides.inSimpleWords: For piecewise functions, check if both pieces meet at the junction point.

slides.title: Challenge: Piecewise Continuity and Differentiability
slides.storyContext: Priya's path function: f(x) = {x² if x < 1; 2x − 1 if x ≥ 1}. Is it continuous and differentiable at x=1?

example.problem: Check continuity and differentiability at x=1.
example.solution: Continuity: f(1) = 2(1)−1 = 1. lim_{x→1⁻} x² = 1. lim_{x→1⁺} (2x−1) = 1. All equal, so continuous. Differentiability: f'₋(1) = 2(1) = 2 (derivative of x²). f'₊(1) = 2 (derivative of 2x−1). Both equal, so differentiable.

slides.inSimpleWords: Check continuity at the junction (all pieces meet). Check if left and right derivatives match. If yes to both, smooth transition.

slides.title: Removable vs. Non-Removable Discontinuities
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Singh clarifies types of breaks: some can be "fixed" (holes), others cannot (jumps or infinite).

points.label: Removable discontinuity
points.text: Limit exists, but f(c) undefined or doesn't match. Example: f(x) = (x²−1)/(x−1) at x=1. Limit is 2, but f(1) undefined.

points.label: Jump discontinuity
points.text: Left and right limits differ. Example: floor function at integer points.

points.label: Infinite discontinuity
points.text: Limit is infinite. Example: f(x) = 1/(x−2) at x=2. Vertical asymptote.

slides.inSimpleWords: Removable: hole. Non-removable: jump or asymptote. Derivatives don't exist at non-removable breaks.

slides.title: The Hole vs. The Jump
slides.storyContext: Priya imagines two different breaks on her running path. The removable one: a small hole (she could jump over, the terrain 'wants' to be continuous). The jump: a cliff edge (truly broken, no way to make it continuous by filling a hole).

example.problem: Removable: f(x) = (x²−4)/(x−2) at x=2. Non-removable: f(x) = {x if x<2; x+1 if x≥2} at x=2.
example.solution: Removable: (x²−4)/(x−2) = (x−2)(x+2)/(x−2) = x+2. Limit at x=2 is 4, but f(2) undefined. Jump: lim_{x→2⁻} x = 2, lim_{x→2⁺} (x+1) = 3. Left ≠ right, irreversible.

slides.inSimpleWords: Removable can be 'fixed' by redefining one point. Jumps and asymptotes cannot.

slides.title: All Three Derivative Rules Applied
slides.storyContext: Priya practices using power, product, and chain rules on a complex expression.

example.problem: Find d/dx[√(3x² + 2)·e^x].

slides.inSimpleWords: Chain rule for complicated inner functions, product rule when multiplying, simplify the result.

slides.title: Challenge: Complete Derivative Computation
slides.storyContext: Priya computes the derivative of a complex function using multiple rules, then finds the slope at a specific point.

example.problem: Find d/dx[(2x³ − 5) · cos(x)] at x=π. Then find the instantaneous rate of change at that point.
example.solution: Using product rule: f'(x) = (6x²)·cos(x) + (2x³−5)·(−sin(x)) = 6x²cos(x) − (2x³−5)sin(x). At x=π: f'(π) = 6π²·cos(π) − (2π³−5)·sin(π) = 6π²·(−1) − (2π³−5)·0 = −6π².

slides.inSimpleWords: Combine rules (product, chain) to differentiate, then substitute the x-value for the specific rate.

slides.title: Challenge: Piecewise with Jump
slides.storyContext: Priya encounters a truly discontinuous path: a cliff with no smooth bridge. Check continuity and differentiability.

example.problem: f(x) = {2x if x<3; x+3 if x≥3}. Continuous and differentiable at x=3?
example.solution: Continuity: f(3) = 3+3 = 6. lim_{x→3⁻} 2x = 6. lim_{x→3⁺} (x+3) = 6. All equal — continuous! Differentiability: f'₋(3) = 2. f'₊(3) = 1. Not equal — not differentiable (smooth meeting, but different slopes).

slides.inSimpleWords: A function can be continuous but not differentiable if the slopes don't match at the junction.

slides.title: What Priya Learned
slides.storyContext: Calculus explains the smoothness and speed of Priya's running path and any motion.

points.text: Continuity: no jumps, holes, or breaks. Three conditions: f(c) defined, limit exists, limit = f(c).
Derivative: instantaneous rate of change, slope of tangent line. f'(c) = lim_{h→0} (f(c+h)−f(c))/h.
Key rules: power, product, chain, quotient — shortcuts to compute derivatives without limits.
Differentiable ⟹ continuous. But continuous ≠ differentiable (corners break differentiability).
Sharp corners have unequal left/right derivatives. Smooth points have matching left/right derivatives.
Position derivatives give velocity, velocity derivatives give acceleration.

slides.inSimpleWords: Continuous functions don't break. Differentiable functions are smooth. Derivatives measure instantaneous rate of change.

subject: Mathematics
title: Ananya's Business Optimization
hook: Ananya runs a small business making Indian snacks. Derivatives help her maximize profit and minimize waste.

slides.title: Application of Derivatives
slides.storyContext: Ananya's ladoo production factory gets x kilos of ghee per day. Profit depends on x. Too little ghee = low profit; too much = waste. Derivatives find the optimal x.

slides.title: The Ladoo Factory
slides.storyContext: Ananya's daily profit function: P(x) = −2x² + 100x − 500 (x = kilos of ghee, P = profit in rupees). Vikram says: derivatives find the maximum profit point. Where should she buy exactly the right amount of ghee?

slides.title: Why Optimization Matters
slides.storyContext: Ananya observes: With 10 kg ghee, profit = −2(100) + 100(10) − 500 = 300 rupees. With 20 kg, profit = −2(400) + 100(20) − 500 = 700 rupees. With 30 kg, profit = −2(900) + 100(30) − 500 = 500 rupees. There's a sweet spot! Vikram says: that's what derivatives find.

points.label: Too little input
points.text: Underutilized resources, low profit.

points.label: Too much input
points.text: Waste and inefficiency, profit drops.

points.label: The optimal point
points.text: Maximum profit exists somewhere in between. Derivatives pinpoint it.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every business has an optimal operating point. Derivatives find it automatically.

slides.title: Critical Points and Extrema
slides.storyContext: Prof. Nair teaches: To find max/min, take the derivative, set it to zero, solve for x.

points.label: Critical point
points.text: Point where f'(x) = 0 or f'(x) doesn't exist.

points.label: First Derivative Test
points.text: At x=c: if f' changes from + to −, it's a maximum. If − to +, it's a minimum. If no change, it's neither.

points.label: Second Derivative Test
points.text: If f''(c) > 0, c is a minimum. If f''(c) < 0, c is a maximum.

example.problem: Find max/min of P(x) = −2x² + 100x − 500.

slides.inSimpleWords: Maximum = peak of a hill (derivative 0, second derivative negative). Minimum = valley (derivative 0, second derivative positive).

slides.title: Finding Critical Points Step-by-Step
slides.storyContext: Ananya works through finding the optimal ghee amount herself, following Prof. Nair's steps.

example.problem: For P(x) = −2x² + 100x − 500, find the critical point and verify it's a maximum.
example.solution: Step 1: P'(x) = −4x + 100. Step 2: Set to zero: −4x + 100 = 0 ⟹ x = 25. Step 3: Check second derivative: P''(x) = −4. Since P''(25) = −4 < 0, it's a maximum. Step 4: Max profit = P(25) = 750 rupees at x = 25 kg ghee.

slides.inSimpleWords: Differentiate, set equal to zero, solve. Then check the second derivative to confirm max or min.

slides.title: Increasing and Decreasing Functions
slides.storyContext: Ananya checks: as x increases from 0, does profit grow or shrink? The sign of f'(x) tells.

points.label: f'(x) > 0
points.text: Function is increasing. Profit rises as ghee amount rises.

points.label: f'(x) < 0
points.text: Function is decreasing. Profit falls as ghee amount rises.

points.label: Finding intervals
points.text: Solve f'(x) = 0 to find critical points. Test signs of f' in each interval.

example.problem: For P(x) = −2x² + 100x − 500, find where it's increasing and decreasing.
example.solution: P'(x) = −4x + 100. P'(x) = 0 at x=25. For x < 25: P'(x) > 0 (increasing). For x > 25: P'(x) < 0 (decreasing). Max profit at x=25.

slides.inSimpleWords: Derivative tells the direction: positive = up, negative = down, zero = flat (peak or valley).

slides.title: Profit Landscape: Before and After the Peak
slides.storyContext: Ananya tests profit at various ghee levels. From 0 to 25 kg: profit climbs (P' > 0). From 25 kg onward: profit falls (P' < 0). The turning point is her sweet spot.

points.label: x = 0 to 25
points.text: Increasing. Each extra kg of ghee boosts profit.

points.label: x = 25
points.text: The peak. Profit reaches 750 rupees.

points.label: x = 25 onward
points.text: Decreasing. Extra ghee means waste and lower profit.

slides.inSimpleWords: The derivative sign (+ or −) tells if the function is climbing or falling.

slides.title: Concavity and Inflection Points
slides.storyContext: Prof. Nair introduces curvature: Does the curve bend upward (concave up) or downward (concave down)?

points.label: f''(x) > 0
points.text: Concave up. Graph looks like ⌢ (minimum at critical point).

points.label: f''(x) < 0
points.text: Concave down. Graph looks like ⌣ (maximum at critical point).

points.label: Inflection point
points.text: Where f''(x) = 0 and changes sign. Curve changes concavity.

example.problem: For f(x) = x³ − 3x² + 2, find inflection points.
example.solution: f'(x) = 3x² − 6x. f''(x) = 6x − 6. Set f''(x) = 0: 6x − 6 = 0 ⟹ x = 1. f''(0) = −6 < 0 (concave down left). f''(2) = 6 > 0 (concave up right). Inflection at x=1.

slides.inSimpleWords: Second derivative tells curvature. Zero and sign change = inflection point (curve flips from cup to cap).

slides.title: Concavity of Ananya's Profit Function
slides.storyContext: Ananya computes the second derivative of her profit function to understand its shape.

example.problem: For P(x) = −2x² + 100x − 500, find P''(x) and interpret concavity.
example.solution: P'(x) = −4x + 100. P''(x) = −4. Since P''(x) = −4 < 0 everywhere, the function is concave down everywhere. Parabola opens downward — any critical point is a maximum.

slides.inSimpleWords: Negative second derivative means the curve domes downward — any peak is a maximum.

slides.title: Optimization in Real Life
slides.storyContext: Vikram shares business scenarios where derivatives solve practical problems.

points.label: Minimize cost
points.text: Find dimensions of a packaging box that minimizes material (surface area) for fixed volume.

points.label: Maximize revenue
points.text: Find the price/quantity that maximizes profit = revenue − cost.

points.label: Minimize time
points.text: Find the optimal speed to minimize travel time + fuel cost.

slides.inSimpleWords: Set up function (cost, profit, time), take derivative, set to zero, solve. Second derivative confirms max or min.

slides.title: Monotonicity and First Derivative Test
slides.storyContext: Prof. Nair shows how to analyze when profit is increasing or decreasing without computing exact values.

points.label: f'(x) > 0 on (a,b)
points.text: f is strictly increasing on that interval. Buy more resources, profit grows.

points.label: f'(x) < 0 on (a,b)
points.text: f is strictly decreasing on that interval. Add more, profit shrinks.

points.label: Critical point analysis
points.text: Sign change of f' from + to − indicates a local maximum. − to + indicates local minimum.

slides.inSimpleWords: Derivative sign tells if function is rising or falling. Sign change marks a peak or valley.

slides.title: Analyzing Monotonicity over an Interval
slides.storyContext: Ananya analyzes her profit function over different ranges of production.

example.problem: For P(x) = −x² + 20x − 50, find where P is increasing and decreasing. Identify critical point.
example.solution: P'(x) = −2x + 20. P'(x) = 0 at x = 10. For x < 10: P'(x) > 0 (increasing). For x > 10: P'(x) < 0 (decreasing). Local max at x = 10.

slides.inSimpleWords: Test the sign of the derivative in each region. Rising region: derivative positive. Falling region: derivative negative.

slides.title: Applied Calculus in Business: Elasticity
slides.storyContext: Vikram introduces price elasticity of demand: how sensitive demand is to price changes. Derivatives measure this sensitivity.

points.label: Elasticity formula
points.text: E = (dq/dp) · (p/q), where q is quantity and p is price.

points.label: Elastic (E > 1)
points.text: Demand is very sensitive to price. Small price increase → big quantity drop.

points.label: Inelastic (E < 1)
points.text: Demand is insensitive to price. Price change → small quantity change.

slides.inSimpleWords: Elasticity: how much quantity changes when price changes. Derivatives measure the sensitivity.

slides.title: Real Optimization Success
slides.storyContext: Ananya applies derivatives to three problems: (1) Maximize profit from ghee supply, (2) minimize packaging cost for a fixed volume of ladoos, (3) find the optimal selling price for maximum revenue.

points.label: Profit optimization
points.text: She finds 25 kg ghee maximizes daily profit at 750 rupees.

points.label: Cost optimization
points.text: She finds box dimensions that minimize material waste.

points.label: Revenue optimization
points.text: She finds the price point that maximizes total revenue.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every optimization follows the same pattern: set up the function, differentiate, find critical points, verify max/min.

slides.title: Box Optimization Problem
slides.storyContext: Ananya needs to ship ladoos in boxes. She has a rectangular sheet 20 cm × 30 cm. She'll cut squares of side x from corners, fold up, and tape. What x maximizes volume?

example.problem: Maximize V(x) = x(20−2x)(30−2x).

slides.inSimpleWords: Write volume in terms of x, find where derivative = 0, check which solution is in valid range, calculate max volume.

slides.title: Motion: Speed, Acceleration, Distance
slides.storyContext: Ananya's delivery bike position: s(t) = t³ − 6t² + 9t (meters, t in seconds). What's instantaneous speed at t=2? Is the bike speeding up or slowing down?

points.label: Velocity = ds/dt
points.text: Speed at a moment.

points.label: Acceleration = dv/dt = d²s/dt²
points.text: How fast speed is changing.

example.problem: Find velocity and acceleration at t=2.
example.solution: v(t) = s'(t) = 3t² − 12t + 9. At t=2: v(2) = 12 − 24 + 9 = −3 m/s (moving backward). a(t) = v'(t) = 6t − 12. At t=2: a(2) = 12 − 12 = 0 m/s² (no acceleration at this instant).

slides.inSimpleWords: Derivative of position = velocity. Derivative of velocity = acceleration. Second derivative of position = acceleration.

slides.title: Revenue and Profit Optimization
slides.storyContext: Ananya studies how to maximize her revenue by adjusting the selling price and quantity relationship.

example.problem: Revenue = price × quantity. If demand q = 100 − 2p (p = price), find dR/dp and interpret.
example.solution: Revenue R(p) = p·q = p(100−2p) = 100p − 2p². dR/dp = 100 − 4p. Setting to zero: 100 − 4p = 0 ⟹ p = 25. Revenue is maximized at price = 25 rupees, yielding q = 100 − 50 = 50 units, R = 1250 rupees.

slides.inSimpleWords: Express revenue in terms of price, differentiate, set to zero to find optimal price.

slides.title: Challenge: Multi-step Optimization
slides.storyContext: Ananya sells ladoos at price p rupees per box. Daily demand q = 500 − 10p boxes. Cost per box is 20 rupees. Find price p that maximizes profit.

example.problem: Profit = (revenue) − (cost) = (p·q) − (20·q). Find optimal p.

slides.inSimpleWords: Express profit as function of price/quantity, differentiate, set to zero, solve. Check second derivative for max/min.

slides.title: Local vs. Global Extrema
slides.storyContext: Prof. Nair explains: A function may have multiple peaks and valleys. Some are local (peaks/valleys in a region), others are global (highest/lowest everywhere).

points.label: Local maximum
points.text: f(c) ≥ f(x) for all x near c, but not necessarily globally.

points.label: Global (absolute) maximum
points.text: f(c) ≥ f(x) for ALL x in the domain.

points.label: Finding them
points.text: Check critical points, test second derivative, also check boundaries if domain is restricted.

slides.inSimpleWords: Local max: peak on a hill. Global max: highest point in the entire landscape. Boundaries matter.

slides.title: Local Max vs. Global Max
slides.storyContext: Ananya's profit function has multiple peaks. She needs to find the global maximum to decide production.

example.problem: f(x) = x³ − 3x² + 2 on [−1, 3]. Find all critical points and determine global max/min.
example.solution: f'(x) = 3x² − 6x = 3x(x−2). Critical points: x = 0, x = 2. f(−1) = −1−3+2 = −2. f(0) = 2 (local max). f(2) = 8−12+2 = −2 (local min). f(3) = 27−27+2 = 2. Global max = f(0) = 2. Global min = f(2) = −2 or f(−1) = −2 or f(3) = 2 — check all.

slides.inSimpleWords: Evaluate critical points and boundaries. The highest value is global max; lowest is global min.

slides.title: Rolle's Theorem and Mean Value Theorem
slides.storyContext: Prof. Nair introduces theoretical cornerstones: if a smooth function has the same height at two points, there's a flat point in between.

points.label: Rolle's Theorem
points.text: If f is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and f(a) = f(b), then ∃c ∈ (a,b) where f'(c) = 0.

points.label: Mean Value Theorem (MVT)
points.text: If f is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), then ∃c where f'(c) = (f(b)−f(a))/(b−a).

points.label: Interpretation
points.text: Average rate of change equals instantaneous rate at some point.

slides.inSimpleWords: Rolle: if endpoints match, there's a flat spot inside. MVT: average slope equals some instantaneous slope.

slides.title: Applying Rolle's Theorem
slides.storyContext: Ananya's position function: s(t) = t² − 4t + 5. At t=1, s(1)=2. At t=3, s(3)=2. There must be a moment when velocity is zero.

example.problem: Verify Rolle's Theorem for f(x) = x² − 4x + 5 on [1,3].
example.solution: f(1) = 1−4+5 = 2. f(3) = 9−12+5 = 2. f is continuous and differentiable. f'(x) = 2x−4. Set f'(c) = 0: 2c−4 = 0 ⟹ c = 2. Indeed, 1 < 2 < 3, so Rolle's Theorem applies.

slides.inSimpleWords: If a function starts and ends at the same height, it must have a flat point (zero derivative) somewhere in between.

slides.title: Challenge: Constrained Optimization
slides.storyContext: Ananya must minimize the cost of a cylindrical ladoo container with volume 1 liter (1000 cm³). If material costs 0.01 rupees per cm², what are optimal radius and height?

example.problem: Minimize surface area of cylinder with fixed volume V = 1000 cm³. (S = 2πr² + 2πrh, and V = πr²h).
example.solution: From V = πr²h = 1000, get h = 1000/(πr²). Substitute into S: S(r) = 2πr² + 2πr·(1000/(πr²)) = 2πr² + 2000/r. dS/dr = 4πr − 2000/r² = 0 ⟹ 4πr³ = 2000 ⟹ r³ = 500/π ⟹ r ≈ 4.92 cm. Then h = 1000/(π·(4.92)²) ≈ 13.15 cm.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use the constraint to eliminate one variable, then optimize the resulting single-variable function.

slides.title: Challenge: Related Rates Problem
slides.storyContext: Ananya observes: as she increases production speed, the cost per unit changes. If she increases production rate by 10 boxes/hour, how fast does her total hourly cost change?

example.problem: Cost C = 100 + 0.5q², where q is production rate (boxes/hour). If dq/dt = 2 boxes/hour², find dC/dt when q = 50.
example.solution: dC/dq = q. At q = 50: dC/dq = 50. By chain rule: dC/dt = (dC/dq)·(dq/dt) = 50·2 = 100 rupees/hour². Cost is rising at 100 rupees per hour squared.

slides.inSimpleWords: Chain rule for related rates: find how one quantity changes based on another using derivatives.

slides.title: Real-World Optimization: Ananya's Complete Case Study
slides.storyContext: Ananya combines all optimization tools: profit function, critical points, second derivative test, and boundary checks to find maximum profit over a realistic production range.

example.problem: Ananya's daily profit: P(x) = −0.5x² + 80x − 500 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 150. Find global maximum profit and optimal production.

slides.inSimpleWords: For bounded domains, always check critical points AND boundaries. Choose the true global maximum.

slides.title: What Ananya Learned
slides.storyContext: Calculus turned Ananya into an optimizer, running her business with mathematical precision.

points.text: Critical points: f'(x) = 0. Find them to locate max/min.
First Derivative Test: derivative changes sign at critical point. + to − = max, − to + = min.
Second Derivative Test: f''(c) < 0 ⟹ max, f''(c) > 0 ⟹ min.
Concavity: f''(x) > 0 = concave up. f''(x) < 0 = concave down. Inflection = sign change of f''.
Real applications: optimize dimensions (volume, area), price (profit, revenue), motion (velocity, acceleration).
Constrained optimization: use the constraint to reduce variables, then apply standard optimization.

slides.inSimpleWords: Derivatives find where functions peak and valley. Critical business tool for profit, cost, and efficiency.
